n1: The board from figure thirteen says one bead can start and ten wait. Something has to work it the way a team would: take what's ready, build it, have someone else read it before it lands, and pick up whatever that unblocked. In Keelson that's a swarm: a lead agent that owns the outcome, workers it spawns as the work calls for them, and a channel they all talk in.
n2: In the swarm launcher, paste the brief and the factory prompt, and pick Fleet: a lead and up to seven workers.
n3: Factory mode drops the turn and clock budgets. It runs as long as work keeps landing.
n4: Writers may change files, each in its own git worktree, and the lead may use the tracker.
n6: The factory prompt asks for three things one agent can't do to itself. Others critique the plan before anyone builds. A design critic judges every visible change from screenshots, and sends back one fix at a time. And no head merges until an agent other than its writer approves it. These are real lines from the channel.
n7: Twenty four minutes in, seven beads have shipped, and two writers build side by side as the graph widens.
n8: Then the board drains. Eleven of eleven, shipped.
n9: Forty six minutes, a hundred ninety turns, about twelve dollars at list price.
n10: On main, the writers' branches merged one by one.
n11: And this is what they built. Cosmos, a planetarium at night. The filters live in the URL, and every object has its own illustration.
n12: A workflow runs one plan in one order, and that's right when you know the plan. A factory reads the graph, staffs itself, and checks its own work, so you get the review a team would give without being the bottleneck.
n13: Ready work in. Reviewed work out.
n14: Keelson. Lay the keel, raise the ribs.
n10b: And a hundred twenty tests pass.
n11b: A chill, counted on the server.
